openers.eco: Beneath every economy lies a living one. Soil, a mix of minerals, organic matter, water, air and organisms, supports the plants that people and animals eat, and its power to give steady harvests can rise or fall. On land, and in the sunlit surface of oceans and lakes, plants and tiny drifting organisms turn carbon dioxide into the organic matter that almost everything else feeds on. This part of the course follows how that living matter is made, weighed and passed along, and how groups of each species grow, shrink and interact. It also meets the movement that grew up to protect it all.
openers.ecosystem-structure-and-function: An ecosystem has parts, and it does work. Some parts are alive: plants and algae that make their own food from sunlight, and the animals, fungi and microbes that must get their carbon from others. Other parts are not alive at all, such as water, light, temperature and the soil, a mixture of minerals, organic matter, gases, water and organisms. The work is the steady making of new living matter, measured by how much mass an area holds and how fast it adds more. This chapter starts with the soil underfoot and the drifting organisms of the sea, then follows how groups of one species change through births, deaths and movement.

nature-eco-387.title: Soil: the crowded living layer beneath every harvest
nature-eco-387.text: A single gram of soil can hold billions of organisms from thousands of species. Most of them are microbes, and most remain largely unexplored. One recent study suggested that soil is home to 59 ± 15% of all the species on Earth. Soil is a mixture of minerals, organic matter, gases, water and living things that together support plant and soil life. Scientists call it a three-phase system. A solid frame of minerals and organic matter is laced with pores that hold gases, and water moves through it carrying dissolved substances. That mixture does a great deal of work. Soil is a habitat, a recycler of nutrients and wastes, a regulator of water quality and of the atmosphere, and the medium in which plants grow. Those jobs make it a key provider of ecosystem services. Its texture, set by the shares of sand, silt and clay, is the most important physical property for services such as growing crops. The stakes are ancient. Civilizations have prospered or declined according to how much good soil they had and how productive it was.

nature-eco-314.title: Environmentalism: from factory smoke to a global movement
nature-eco-314.text: In 1863 Britain passed the Alkali Acts, the first large-scale modern laws to protect the environment. They answered the rising smoke pollution of the Industrial Revolution, and from that smoke grew environmentalism. It is a broad philosophy and social movement that seeks to protect living things, habitats and the wider environment. It argues for preserving, restoring and improving nature, including systems such as the climate. In practice it often means controlling pollution or protecting biodiversity. At its core it tries to balance people's dealings with the natural systems they depend on, so that all of them can last. In 1972, 113 nations met in Stockholm for the UN Conference on the Human Environment, which led to the UN Environment Programme. The movement has many strands, including {{ref:nature-eco-315}}, {{ref:nature-eco-316}}, evangelical environmentalism and the {{ref:nature-hist-014}}. It also gave rise to green parties. Critics say early environmentalism mostly reflected white middle- and upper-class interests. It overlooked indigenous communities and nearby low-income residents. The cause carries real danger: every year more than 100 environmental activists are murdered worldwide.

nature-eco-398.title: Soil fertility: the power to give steady harvests
nature-eco-398.text: A fertile soil does more than grow one good crop. It gives steady, good-quality yields, and that ability to support plant growth is called soil fertility. Such a soil supplies essential nutrients and water in adequate amounts, and it is free of toxic substances. Several properties help: enough depth for roots, good drainage and air flow, a topsoil rich in organic matter, and a pH of 5.5 to 7.0. The pH scale measures how acidic or alkaline something is. Water can undo the good work. About 18% of the world's cropland is irrigated, and watering with salty, alkaline or acidic water can strip useful salts or build up harmful ones. Studies find a clear statistical link between how much decaying organic matter a soil holds and how fertile it is.

nature-eco-324.title: Autotrophs: the organisms that never need to eat
nature-eco-324.text: Every animal alive depends on organisms that never eat anything. These are autotrophs: organisms that turn non-living energy, such as sunlight or chemicals, into energy stored in organic compounds that others can use. They build carbohydrates, fats and proteins from the carbon in simple substances such as carbon dioxide. Plants on land and algae in water are the producers that every feeding chain starts from. They need no living source of carbon or energy. Organisms that must feed on others, including all animals and almost all fungi, rely on autotrophs for both raw materials and fuel. The whole system runs on a thin margin: plants can use only about 1% of the sun's energy for {{ref:nature-eco-190}}. The German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank coined the term in 1892. Researchers think the first cells on Earth were autotrophs, possibly living at deep-sea hydrothermal vents, hot springs on the ocean floor.

nature-eco-302.title: Primary production: where almost all life's food begins
nature-eco-302.text: Almost every living thing on Earth depends, directly or indirectly, on a single process. Primary production is the making of organic compounds from carbon dioxide in air or water. It happens mainly through {{ref:nature-eco-190}}, the capture of sunlight by plants and algae. The organisms that do it are called primary producers, or autotrophs. They form the base of every feeding chain: mostly plants on land and algae in water. A small share runs on chemosynthesis instead. Chemosynthesis draws energy from chemical reactions of non-living compounds rather than from light. On land, production depends mainly on water and temperature. That is why deserts and polar regions produce so little. Satellites now let scientists add up the whole planet. Their estimate is 104.9 petagrams of carbon a year, with 56.4 made on land and 48.5 in the oceans. The sea, worked by drifting algae, nearly matches the land. Human societies are part of this cycle of production. Yet they influence it far out of proportion to their share of it.

nature-eco-326.title: Biomass: weighing all the life on Earth
nature-eco-326.text: By 2020, the mass of everything humans have made was projected to surpass the mass of all life on Earth. That living total is biomass: the mass of organisms in a given area or ecosystem at a particular time. It can be weighed wet, dry, or as organic carbon, depending on the purpose. In 2018 Earth's live biomass was estimated at about 550 billion tonnes of carbon, mostly in plants. Plants hold 450 billion tonnes of it, and bacteria plus the similar single-celled archaea hold 30. Animals make up less than 0.5% of the total. The sea breaks the pattern. Ocean producers make almost half of each year's new growth, yet they hold only about 0.2% of all biomass. On land, biomass falls sharply at each step up the ladder of who eats whom, but in the oceans it can rise. Wild land mammals are believed to weigh seven times less than in prehistoric times, and livestock now outweigh all wild mammals together.

nature-eco-372.title: Phytoplankton: the invisible half of the world's plant work
nature-eco-372.text: At least half of Earth's oxygen comes from organisms too small to see. Phytoplankton are tiny drifting organisms in oceans and lakes that make their own food by capturing sunlight. Because they need light, they live in the sunlit surface layer of the water. They carry out about half of global {{ref:nature-eco-190}}, though they make up only about 1% of global plant biomass. Marine phytoplankton fix about 50 Pg, or petagrams, of carbon a year. They are the base of the feeding networks of sea and lake. They also drive the {{ref:nature-eco-204}}, which moves carbon to the deep ocean. They include cyanobacteria and single-celled protists such as diatoms, and about 5,000 marine species are known. They turn over in days rather than decades, so they respond quickly to a changing climate. Warming splits the water into layers that mix less, cutting their nutrient supply and their output. Some studies indicate that their global density has fallen over the past century.

nature-eco-320.title: Abiotic components: the non-living rules of life
nature-eco-320.text: A rainforest and a desert differ above all in water, and that one difference limits which species can live in each. Water is an abiotic component of an ecosystem: one of the non-living chemical and physical parts of the environment that affect living things. Others include light, temperature, humidity, acidity, salinity (saltiness), altitude, minerals, tides, dissolved oxygen and soil. Such differences also shape how species compete. Humans now create and change these factors. Fertilizers alter the places species live, and heat-trapping gases ({{ref:nature-eco-162}}) change the ocean's pH, its acidity. Non-living factors can even steer evolution. Salinity, for instance, can give one species an edge over another, and that pressure can lead to new species.

nature-eco-374.title: Population: one species, one place, one time
nature-eco-374.text: Ecologists rarely count a large population in full. Methods such as the Lincoln index instead estimate the total from the individuals actually seen. In ecology, a population is a group of organisms of the same species living in a particular place at a particular time. A description usually names who belongs to it, its size, the area it occupies and the period studied. Ecologists stress individuals interacting and competing in one area. An evolutionary view stresses genes and reproduction instead. Populations of different species living and interacting together make up a {{ref:nature-eco-331}}. Separate populations of one species, spread out in space, can be treated as a larger unit: a {{ref:nature-eco-379}}.

nature-eco-362.title: Heterotrophs: life that must feed on other life
nature-eco-362.text: Every mushroom is a heterotroph, and so are most animals. A heterotroph is an organism that cannot make its own food. It gets its carbon from other organisms or from their remains. The group includes most animals, all fungi, some bacteria and protists, and many parasitic plants. In the chain of who eats whom, heterotrophs are the consumers. Autotrophs, which make food from sunlight or inorganic chemicals, are the producers. Detritivores are heterotrophs that eat dead plants, dead animals and feces. Their work keeps the planet's materials moving. Respiration by heterotrophic microbes releases much of the carbon dioxide entering the atmosphere, which plants then reuse. Through mineralization, the release of nutrients locked in dead matter, heterotrophs turn organic nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus into inorganic forms that plants can use. That step is critical to plant survival and to soil fertility.

nature-eco-375.title: Population ecology: births, deaths, arrivals and departures
nature-eco-375.text: A population changes in only four ways: individuals are born, die, arrive or leave. Population ecology studies those changes, through births, deaths, immigration and emigration, and how populations interact with their environment. Its bookkeeping fits on one line: N1 = N0 + B − D + I − E. The new number is the starting number, plus births, minus deaths, plus immigrants, minus emigrants. Population size is the number of individuals, and population density is how closely packed they are. The largest population an environment's resources can sustain is its {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. The field began with Malthus's model, in which a population in a constant environment grows or declines exponentially. Fisheries and wildlife managers track three rates: {{ref:nature-eco-590}}, growth and mortality, including deaths from harvesting. Population viability analysis also grew from this field. It predicts a species' long-term chance of persisting in a patch of suitable land, and it matters for conservation.

nature-eco-383.title: Ecological productivity: how fast an ecosystem grows
nature-eco-383.text: Swamps and marshes are listed as producing 2,500 grams of carbon in new biomass on each square meter every year. That figure measures ecological productivity: the rate at which an ecosystem makes new biomass. It is often given in grams per square meter per day. The productivity of plants and other autotrophs is called primary productivity. That of animals and other heterotrophs is secondary productivity. Three things set it: nutrient supply, temperature and water. More is not always better. Nutrients washed in from fertilizer can trigger algal blooms, sudden surges of algae. These raise primary production but leave the ecosystem less stable.

nature-eco-391.title: Soil degradation: five ways soil loses its power
nature-eco-391.text: Soil can wear out. Soil degradation is the decline of soil's ability to do its jobs, and it happens in five main ways. Soil can become more acidic. It can be contaminated or eroded. It can fill with salt. And dry land can turn to desert, the process covered in {{ref:nature-eco-091}}. That last one is widely misunderstood. Drought alone is a common misconception as its cause. It usually comes from poorly adapted human activities, such as overgrazing or harvesting too much firewood. Erosion, the wearing away of soil, is driven by water, wind, ice and gravity, and several kinds can strike at once. Salination is a build-up of salts that cuts the farming value of soils and the plants growing on them. Contamination has a partial natural remedy. At low levels, soil organisms can treat it, mainly through enzymes made by microbes.

nature-eco-303.title: Gross and net primary production: what plants keep
nature-eco-303.text: A plant spends part of every sugar it makes just staying alive. Gross primary production is all the chemical energy producers capture in a given time. Net primary production is what remains after they use some for their own respiration, the process that releases stored energy. The net share fuels the producers' growth and reproduction, and it is what plant-eaters can eat. Put simply, net equals gross minus the carbon lost to respiration. Gross production is harder to measure, because respiration constantly uses up some of the sugars as they are made. Scaled-up eddy covariance measurements, which track gases flowing between land and air, give a land gross primary production of 123±8 Gt of carbon a year for 1998-2005. Where there is no light, as in caves and hydrothermal vents, microbes that feed on chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide or methane are the only producers. A wider measure, {{ref:nature-eco-241}}, also subtracts the respiration of consumers.

nature-eco-287.title: Ecosystem ecology: the living and non-living as one system
nature-eco-287.text: In Guatemala's western highlands, forest loss has raised the risk of landslides and water shortages. Totonicapán, which kept its forests, is more economically stable. Ecosystem ecology is the science behind such contrasts. It studies how the living and non-living parts of an ecosystem interact as one integrated system. It focuses on working processes such as primary production, the decay of dead matter, and feeding relationships, which keep ecosystems and their services going. Eugene Odum and {{ref:nature-hist-063}} measured flows of energy and matter through whole ecosystems. Most natural ecosystems are limited by nitrogen. Nutrients recycled from decaying plant litter keep them productive. The field's findings have improved the sustainable production of forage, fiber, fuel and water. They also show the cost of chasing maximum output: intensive fertilizer use in the US Midwest has degraded fisheries in the Gulf of Mexico.

nature-eco-406.title: Terrestrial ecosystems: life on land
nature-eco-406.text: Terrestrial ecosystems cover 144,150,000 km², or 28.26% of Earth's surface. A terrestrial ecosystem is one found on land, such as {{ref:nature-eco-565}}, {{ref:nature-eco-559}}, forest, grassland or desert. It differs from water ecosystems in having soil, not water, at the surface, with plants reaching above it. Water is plentiful in some places and scarce in others. Temperatures also swing more by day and by season than they do in water. The UN goal described in {{ref:nature-gov-030}} targets the conservation, restoration and sustainable use of these ecosystems.

nature-eco-376.title: Exponential and logistic growth: boom without limits, and with them
nature-eco-376.text: Monk parakeets released in the United States multiplied from 1975 to 1994, reaching about 55 times their 1975 numbers. That is exponential growth, one of the two most common models of how populations grow. In it, the growth rate per individual stays constant, so numbers snowball. The model assumes unlimited resources and no predators. The second model, logistic growth, adds a ceiling. Growth slows as numbers approach {{ref:nature-eco-593}}, the most the environment can support. In the classic models, r stands for the intrinsic growth rate and K for that ceiling. Malthus first framed the exponential model, and Verhulst and Gompertz refined it in the early 19th century.

nature-eco-389.title: Cation exchange capacity: how soil holds its nutrients
nature-eco-389.text: Clay particles and decayed organic matter carry electric charges, which let them hold charged particles called ions on their surfaces. Cation exchange capacity is a soil's ability to hold positively charged nutrient ions, or cations, from the soil water and release them later to roots. This holding does several jobs. It steadies the soil's acidity, alters its structure and cleans water seeping through by trapping both useful and harmful cations. It is measured in milliequivalents per 100 grams of dry soil. Base saturation is the share of holding sites taken by cations such as calcium and magnesium.

nature-eco-388.title: Soil composition: half solid, half empty space
nature-eco-388.text: Half of a typical soil is not solid at all. A typical soil is about 45% mineral and 5% organic matter. The other half is pores, split equally between water and gas. The solid share stays roughly constant in the short term. Water and air trade places, so as one rises the other falls. The air in those pores is unusual. Carbon dioxide there may reach 10 to 100 times its 0.04% share of the atmosphere, because roots and microbes use up oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

nature-eco-392.title: Soil horizons: the layers in a soil profile
nature-eco-392.text: Soil is built in layers. Each is a soil horizon: a horizontal layer whose features, composition and age differ from the layers above and below. One layer often signals that a soil has truly formed. In the B horizon, materials washed down from above build up, including clay, decayed organic matter, iron oxide, carbonate and gypsum.

nature-eco-390.title: Soil pH: the acid test of the ground
nature-eco-390.text: Soil pH, a measure of how acidic or alkaline a soil is, runs in practice from 3.5 to 9.5. Life sets those limits, because values beyond them are toxic. Some soils hold their pH steadier than others. This resistance to change, called buffering capacity, rises with {{ref:nature-eco-389}}, the soil's power to hold charged nutrients. Pure sand has almost no buffering capacity at all.

nature-eco-317.title: Anti-environmentalism: the organized opposition
nature-eco-317.text: Environmentalism has organized opponents. Anti-environmentalism covers ideas and actions that oppose environmentalism as a whole or particular environmental policies. It can take the form of an organized countermovement that targets climate science and environmental regulation. Its actors may include workers in industries threatened by environmental policy. They may also include anti-environmentalist think tanks, research groups that promote these views.

nature-eco-315.title: Free-market environmentalism: property rights as protection
nature-eco-315.text: Could a lawsuit protect a river better than a regulation? Free-market environmentalism holds that free markets, property rights and tort law, the law of civil harms, are the best tools for a healthy environment. Its advocates rely on individual and class-action lawsuits to drive out polluters. Clear property rights, they argue, let people bargain for better outcomes and sue to stop harm. They blame environmental problems on laws that blur those rights and on transaction costs too high for bargaining. Critics reply that it cannot handle collective problems: water is hard to privatize and pollution is hard to trace.

nature-eco-316.title: Labor environmentalism: unions take on the environment
nature-eco-316.text: Trade unions are caught between the economic growth model and the global ecological crisis. Labor environmentalism is their response. Unions work to shape environmental policy, campaign on environmental issues and partner with environmental groups. To promote green jobs, they developed the idea of a {{ref:nature-clim-174}}.
